work: Enarratio in Epistolam I B. Pauli ad Timotheum
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio capituli primi: Paulus apostolus Jesu Christi, etc.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, etc.

paras.t: PAULUS apostolus Jesu Christi, secundum imperium, id est ab imperio voluntatis, Dei Salvatoris nostri, videlicet Dei Patris, qui est salvator per auctoritatem et principalem efficientiam, quoniam gratiam influit, et per Filium suum mundum redemit, et Christi Jesu spei nostræ, id est ab imperio Christi factus apostolus, qui Christus est objectum et causa spei nostræ. Voluntas autem Patris et Christi, atque imperium utriusque, unum sunt penitus, sicut et utriusque est una essentia, una potentia, indivisa actio foris transiens, loquendo de Christo in quantum est Deus. Patre autem et Filio ejus volente ac præcipiente, factus est Paulus apostolus: qui scribit Timotheo dilecto filio in fide christiana, quoniam hanc didicit et recepit Timotheus a Paulo dispositive seu instrumentaliter. Sicque Apostolus genuit eum quantum ad esse christianitatis, quod fundatur in fide. [Gratia, misericordia et pax a Deo Patre, et Christo Jesu Domino nostro.]
paras.en: [[1:1|Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ|Paulus apostolus Jesu Christi]], [[1:1|according to the commandment|secundum imperium]], that is, by the command of the will, [[1:1|of God our Saviour|Dei Salvatoris nostri]], namely of God the Father, who is Saviour by authority and as principal efficient cause, since He pours in grace, and through His Son redeemed the world, [[1:1|and Christ Jesus our hope|et Christi Jesu spei nostræ]]: that is, made an apostle by the command of Christ, which Christ is the object and cause of our hope. Now the will of the Father and of Christ, and the command of each, are wholly one, as also there is one essence of each, one power, one undivided action passing outward, speaking of Christ inasmuch as He is God. By the will and precept, then, of the Father and of His Son, Paul was made an apostle: who writes [[1:2|To Timothy, his beloved son in faith|Timotheo dilecto filio in fide]], the Christian faith, since Timothy learnt and received it from Paul dispositively or instrumentally [that is, Paul was the disposing instrument, God the principal cause]. And so the Apostle begot him as to his Christian being, which is founded on faith. [[1:2|Grace, mercy and peace, from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord|Gratia, misericordia et pax a Deo Patre, et Christo Jesu Domino nostro]] [this lemma is printed within brackets in the edition].

paras.t: Et quia inter cetera episcopi officia est, falsam doctrinam exstirpare, seu falsis doctoribus obviare, ideo primo de hoc tractat Apostolus. Sicut rogavi te ex caritate et humilitate, cui præcipere potui apostolica auctoritate, ut remaneres Ephesi, id est in urbe Ephesina metropoli Asiæ minoris, quæ est pars Græciæ, quum irem in Macedoniam: cujus metropolis est Thessalonica, ad Græciam pertinens. Cur autem rogaverit eum, adjecit: ut denuntiares quibusdam, videlicet separatis ab ecclesiastica unitate hominibus, utputa pseudoapostolis et eorum auditoribus, ne aliter docerent, id est, ne aliquid nostræ prædicationi contrarium affirmarent, neque intenderent fabulis, id est fictis et frivolis narrationibus Judæorum, quæ nec sacræ Scripturæ veteris Testamenti nec rationi concordant, et genealogiis interminatis, id est infinitis quodammodo et inexplicabilibus generationibus, quas isti confingunt. De quibus in Talmud eorum plurima conscribuntur, quæ sunt inexplicanda mendacia, scilicet, quod Adam duas habuit conjuges, de quibus plures genuit filios. Ex quibus excæcati Judæi deducunt, conscribunt, et computant interminabiles pene progenies. Quæ fabulæ et genealogiæ, quæstiones litigiosas, vanas ac steriles præstant per occasionem, quia ad eas inducunt, magis quam ædificationem Dei, id est informationem divinam seu spiritualem, quæ ædificatio est in fide tanquam fundamento, et in his quæ fidem concernunt, ad recte intelligendum testimonia fidei, et bene exsequendum seu operandum præcepta fidei atque consilia.
paras.en: And since among the other offices of a bishop is to root out false doctrine, or to withstand false teachers, the Apostle treats of this first. [[1:3|As I desired thee|Sicut rogavi te]] out of charity and humility, though I could have commanded thee by apostolic authority, [[1:3|to remain at Ephesus|ut remaneres Ephesi]], that is, in the city of Ephesus, metropolis of Asia Minor, which is part of Greece, [[1:3|when I went into Macedonia|quum irem in Macedoniam]], whose metropolis is Thessalonica, belonging to Greece. Why he desired him, he adds: [[1:3|that thou mightest charge some|ut denuntiares quibusdam]], namely men separated from the unity of the Church, such as false apostles and their hearers, [[1:3|not to teach otherwise|ne aliter docerent]], that is, not to affirm anything contrary to our preaching, [[1:4|Not to give heed to fables|neque intenderent fabulis]], that is, to the feigned and frivolous tales of the Jews, which agree neither with the holy Scripture of the Old Testament nor with reason, [[1:4|and endless genealogies|et genealogiis interminatis]], that is, generations in a manner infinite and inexplicable, which these men invent. Of these very many things are written in their Talmud, which are lies past unravelling: for instance, that Adam had two wives, of whom he begot many sons. From these the blinded Jews derive, write down and reckon almost endless lines of descent. [[1:4|which furnish questions|Quæ … quæstiones … præstant]] [Denis: “which fables and genealogies furnish questions”], contentious, vain and barren, by occasion, since they lead into them, [[1:4|rather than the edification of God|magis quam ædificationem Dei]], that is, divine or spiritual instruction, [[1:4|which is in faith|quæ ædificatio est in fide]], this edification, as in its foundation, and in the things that concern faith: for rightly understanding the testimonies of faith, and for well carrying out or performing the precepts and counsels of faith.

paras.t: Finis autem, id est finalis perfectio seu consummatio ultimata, præcepti, id est legis divinæ veteris et novæ, imo et omnium præceptorum, est caritas, id est actus interior caritatis, qua Deus proximusque diligitur, procedens de corde puro, id est appetitu intellectivo seu voluntate a passionibus et vitiis expurgata, et conscientia bona, quantum ad intellectum, cujus actus est conscientia, quæ est applicatio scientiæ ad particulare agibile. Quum vero recte applicatur, vocatur conscientia bona. De tali itaque conscientia actualis dilectio oritur, quando videlicet intellectus applicat suam notitiam ad id quod vere amabile est. Et fide non ficta, id est sincera, non simulata. Procedit autem dilectio ex voluntate elicitive, ex actu intellectus ostensive sive directive. Intellectus namque voluntati ostendit quid amet, et cognitio via est ad dilectionem. Ex fide vero [procedit] sicut ex quadam fundamentali radice, actum dilectionis ad supernaturalem finem dirigente. Caritas itaque est finis præcepti, sicut et alio loco testatur Apostolus: Plenitudo legis est dilectio. Unde Salvator in mandatis caritatis legem atque Prophetas censet pendere. Tria quippe præcepta primæ tabulæ ordinantur ad dilectionem Dei. Septem vero præcepta tabulæ secundæ ordinantur ad dilectionem proximi, quam certum est ordinari ad dilectionem Dei, quæ finis et vertex est totius perfectionis. Sed non potest dilectio Dei esse perfecta et pura, nisi passionibus reformatis.
paras.en: [[1:5|Now the end|Finis autem]], that is, the final perfection or ultimate consummation, [[1:5|of the commandment|præcepti]], that is, of the divine law old and new, indeed of all precepts, [[1:5|is charity|est caritas]], that is, the inward act of charity by which God and neighbour are loved, proceeding [[1:5|from a pure heart|de corde puro]], that is, from the intellectual appetite or will purged of passions and vices, [[1:5|and a good conscience|et conscientia bona]], as regards the intellect, whose act is conscience, which is the application of knowledge to a particular thing to be done. When it is rightly applied, it is called a good conscience. From such a conscience, then, actual love arises, namely when the intellect applies its knowledge to what is truly lovable. [[1:5|and an unfeigned faith|Et fide non ficta]], that is, sincere, not pretended. Love proceeds from the will elicitively [that is, as the power that produces the act], from the act of the intellect by way of showing or directing. For the intellect shows the will what to love, and knowledge is the way to love. But from faith it proceeds as from a fundamental root, directing the act of love to a supernatural end. Charity, then, is the end of the commandment, as the Apostle also testifies elsewhere: [[Rom 13:10|Love therefore is the fulfilling of the law|Plenitudo legis est dilectio]]. Hence the Saviour judges that the law and the Prophets depend on the commandments of charity[[Matt 22:40||]]. For the three precepts of the first table are ordered to the love of God; the seven precepts of the second table to the love of neighbour, which certainly is ordered to the love of God, the end and summit of all perfection. But the love of God cannot be perfect and pure unless the passions are reformed.

paras.t: A quibus, videlicet a puro corde, conscientia bona, et fide non ficta, quidam hæretici aberrantes, conversi sunt in vaniloquium, id est ad vanas et falsas assertiones de observatione legalium tempore novæ legis, volentes esse legis doctores, eo quod sint in propriis oculis nimium sapientes; non intelligentes neque quæ loquuntur, id est propria verba. Quum enim asserunt cærimonialia legis nunc observanda, nequaquam intelligunt propriam vocem, quum cærimonialia ex sua natura fuerint figurativa: unde veritate patefacta, cessare debuerant. Neque de quibus affirmant testimonia Scripturarum veteris Testamenti, quibus suum propositum probare nituntur.
paras.en: [[1:6|From which things|A quibus]], namely from a pure heart, a good conscience and unfeigned faith, [[1:6|some, going astray|quidam hæretici aberrantes]], heretics, [[1:6|are turned aside unto vain babbling|conversi sunt in vaniloquium]], that is, to vain and false assertions about observing the legal ceremonies in the time of the new law, [[1:7|Desiring to be teachers of the law|volentes esse legis doctores]], because they are overmuch wise in their own eyes[[Is 5:21||]]; [[1:7|understanding neither the things they say|non intelligentes neque quæ loquuntur]], that is, their own words. For when they assert that the ceremonies of the law are now to be observed, they do not understand their own utterance, since the ceremonies were by their nature figurative, and so, the truth being revealed, they ought to have ceased. [[1:7|nor whereof they affirm|Neque de quibus affirmant]]: the testimonies of the Scriptures of the Old Testament by which they strive to prove their purpose.

paras.t: Scimus autem quia bona est lex Mosaica, non solum in se tanquam divinitus data, sed etiam per comparationem ad homines, si quis ea legitime, id est juste et vere, utatur, intelligendo et observando eam secundum intentionem legislatoris principalis, videlicet Dei, et instrumentalis, utputa angeli seu Moysis, id est, ut spiritualiter intelligatur, ad Christi mysteria ordinetur, et quantum ad præcepta moralia, semper servetur, quantum vero ad cærimonialia, pro tempore legis scriptæ custodienda fuisse noscatur.
paras.en: [[1:8|But we know that the law is good|Scimus autem quia bona est lex]], the law of Moses, not only in itself as given by God, but also in relation to men, [[1:8|if a man use it lawfully|si quis ea legitime]], that is, justly and truly, [[1:8|use it|utatur]], understanding and observing it according to the intention of the principal lawgiver, namely God, and of the instrumental one, such as an angel or Moses: that is, that it be understood spiritually, be ordered to the mysteries of Christ, and as to the moral precepts be always kept, but as to the ceremonial ones be known to have been binding for the time of the written law.

paras.t: Scientes hoc, quia justo, id est bonis hominibus, non est lex posita, id est imposita, divinitusque collata, sed injustis. Videtur huic contrarium quod ait Psalmista: Quis est homo qui timet Dominum? legem statuit ei in via quam elegit. Unde in persona justi loquens: Bonum (inquit) mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti. Baruch quoque ait: Deus invenit omnem viam disciplinæ, dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto sibi. Puer autem et dilectus Dei, est justus. Ad Josue etiam Dominus loquitur: Custodi omnem legem quam tibi præcepit Moyses. Josue autem justus fuit. Et respondendum, quod intentio legis est homines ad debitum finem dirigere. Ideo primus actus legis est, homines facere bonos seu regulare actus humanos. Quantum ad hoc, omnibus data et posita est lex divina, et alia quælibet recta. Denique lex datur per modum præcepti quo applicatur ad actus. Actus vero sunt triplices, scilicet: boni, mali, et indifferentes. Unde et triplex est actus legis, videlicet: præcipere, quoad actus bonos; prohibere, quoad actus malos; et permittere, quoad actus indifferentes. Sunt autem et alii actus legis, videlicet, cogere nolentes, punire prævaricantes, terrere seu pœnas minari. Quantum ad hos actus, non est justis lex posita, nec proprie quantum ad actum prohibitionis. Actus tamen qui vocatur præcipere, cadit super justos: qui subjecti sunt legi, non coacte, sed sponte: non terrore pœnæ, sed amore justitiæ; non subjectione servili, sed libera. Quantum ergo ad hos actus posteriores, non est posita lex justis, sed injustis. Et non subditis, id est perversis et Deo rebellibus.
paras.en: [[1:9|Knowing this: That the law is not made for the just man|Scientes hoc, quia justo]], that is, for good men, [[1:9|the law is not made|non est lex posita]], that is, imposed and conferred by God, [[1:9|but for the unjust|sed injustis]]. Contrary to this seems what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 24:12|Who is the man that feareth the Lord? He hath appointed him a law in the way he hath chosen|Quis est homo qui timet Dominum? legem statuit ei in via quam elegit]]. And speaking in the person of the just man: [[Ps 118:72|The law of thy mouth is good to me, above thousands of gold and silver|Bonum (inquit) mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti]], he says. Baruch also says: [[Bar 3:37|He found out all the way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved|Deus invenit omnem viam disciplinæ, dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto sibi]]. But the servant and beloved of God is the just man. And the Lord says to Josue: [[Jos 1:7|do all the law, which Moses my servant hath commanded thee|Custodi omnem legem quam tibi præcepit Moyses]]. And Josue was just. The answer is that the intention of the law is to direct men to their due end. Hence the first act of law is to make men good, or to regulate human acts; and in this respect the divine law, and every other right law, is given and set for all. Further, law is given by way of precept, by which it is applied to acts. Acts are threefold: good, bad and indifferent. Hence the act of law is threefold: to command, as to good acts; to forbid, as to bad; and to permit, as to indifferent. There are also other acts of law: to compel the unwilling, to punish transgressors, to frighten or threaten penalties. As to these acts the law is not set for the just, nor properly as to the act of prohibition. But the act called commanding does fall upon the just, who are subject to the law not by compulsion but willingly, not by fear of punishment but by love of justice, not by servile but by free subjection. As to these latter acts, therefore, the law is set not for the just but for the unjust. [[1:9|and disobedient|Et non subditis]], that is, the perverse and rebels against God.

paras.t: De quibus particulariter subditur: impiis, qui contra Deum peccant directe, et peccatoribus, qui peccant in proximum, sceleratis in se ipsos, et contaminatis, consentiendo vel cooperando alienis peccatis, parricidis et matricidis, id est parentum carnalium vel spiritualium interfectoribus, homicidis, fornicariis, id est, fornicationem naturalem committentibus, masculorum concubitoribus, quod est peccatum contra naturam, plagiariis, id est, qui alios lædunt, mendacibus, et perjuris; et si (pro quia) quid aliud vitium a prædictis, sanæ doctrinæ, id est veræ atque morali scientiæ, adversatur, huic lex posita est: prout Galatis dixit Apostolus. Lex propter transgressiones posita est. Quæ sana doctrina est tradita secundum Evangelium, id est in Evangelio; vel, Secundum Evangelium, quoniam consonat evangelicæ doctrinæ: Evangelium, dico, gloriæ, id est, quod annuntiat et promittit gloriam, beati Dei, quam Deus gloriosus in se habet, suisque electis communicat; quod Evangelium creditum, id est commissum seu datum, est mihi ut dispensatori, quatenus aliis ipsum annuntiem.
paras.en: Of these it is added in particular: [[1:9|for the ungodly|impiis]], who sin directly against God, [[1:9|and for sinners|et peccatoribus]], who sin against their neighbour, [[1:9|for the wicked|sceleratis]], against themselves, [[1:9|and defiled|et contaminatis]], by consenting to or cooperating in others' sins, [[1:9|for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers|parricidis et matricidis]], that is, slayers of their parents, carnal or spiritual, [[1:9|for manslayers|homicidis]], [[1:10|For fornicators|fornicariis]], that is, those committing natural fornication, [[1:10|for them who defile themselves with mankind|masculorum concubitoribus]], which is the sin against nature, [[1:10|for menstealers|plagiariis]], that is, those who injure others, [[1:10|for liars, for perjured persons|mendacibus, et perjuris]]; [[1:10|and whatever other thing|et si (pro quia) quid aliud]] (*si*, “if”, standing for *quia*) [the Latin reads literally “and if any other”], any vice besides those named, [[1:10|is contrary to sound doctrine|sanæ doctrinæ adversatur]], that is, to true and moral knowledge: for this the law is set, as the Apostle told the Galatians: [[Gal 3:19|It was set because of transgressions|propter transgressiones posita est]]. Which sound doctrine [[1:11|is according to the gospel|est tradita secundum Evangelium]], handed down, that is, in the Gospel; or, according to the Gospel, because it accords with the Gospel teaching: the Gospel, I say, [[1:11|of the glory|gloriæ]], that is, which announces and promises glory, [[1:11|of the blessed God|beati Dei]], which the glorious God has in Himself and communicates to His elect; [[1:11|which hath been committed to my trust|quod … creditum … est mihi]], which Gospel is entrusted or given to me as steward, that I may announce it to others.

paras.t: Gratias ago ei, videlicet Deo Patri, qui me confortavit in anima ad credendum, sperandum, amandum divina, et ad omnia bona agenda, ac mala toleranda, in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, id est per Christum mediatorem Dei ac hominum, per cujus gratiam et meritum confortatus sum; quia fidelem me existimavit, id est, prævidit seu existimando effecit, ponens in ministerio, id est in apostolatus officio ad docendum ac prædicandum. Qui prius, id est, antequam inter Jerusalem et Damascum Christum vidi et credidi, fui blasphemus, Christum negando, et persecutor primitivæ Ecclesiæ, et contumeliosus, id est injurias contumaciter inferens sanctis. Sed ideo misericordiam Dei, id est indulgentiam, gratiam et apostolatum, consecutus sum accidenter, non directe, quia ignorans feci in incredulitate, id est, ignoranter peccavi per infidelitatem, sicque peccatum meum excusabile fuit. Non tamen ignorantia hæc, causa fuit meritoria gratiæ mihi concessæ, sed quædam occasio. Superabundavit autem gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi in me, cum fide et dilectione, id est, etiam fides atque dilectio, quæ est in Christo Jesu sicut in causa et objecto, mihi abundanter infusæ sunt: sicut et alibi dixi, Ubi abundavit iniquitas, superabundavit et gratia.
paras.en: [[1:12|I give him thanks|Gratias ago ei]], namely God the Father, [[1:12|who hath strengthened me|qui me confortavit]] in soul to believe, hope and love divine things, to do all good and bear all evil, [[1:12|even to Christ Jesus our Lord|in Christo Jesu Domino nostro]] [Denis reads “in Christ Jesus”], that is, through Christ the mediator of God and men[[1 Tim 2:5||]], by whose grace and merit I was strengthened; [[1:12|for that he hath counted me faithful|quia fidelem me existimavit]], that is, foresaw it, or by so accounting made me so, [[1:12|putting me in the ministry|ponens in ministerio]], that is, in the office of the apostolate, to teach and preach. [[1:13|Who before|Qui prius]], that is, before I saw and believed in Christ between Jerusalem and Damascus, [[1:13|was a blasphemer|fui blasphemus]], denying Christ, [[1:13|and a persecutor|et persecutor]] of the primitive Church, [[1:13|and contumelious|et contumeliosus]], that is, insolently inflicting injuries on the saints[[Acts 9:1||]][[Acts 7:59||]][[Acts 8:3||]]. [[1:13|But I obtained the mercy of God|Sed … misericordiam Dei … consecutus sum]] [Denis: “But therefore I obtained”], that is, pardon, grace and the apostolate, accidentally, not directly, [[1:13|because I did it ignorantly in unbelief|quia ignorans feci in incredulitate]], that is, I sinned ignorantly through unbelief, and so my sin was excusable. Yet this ignorance was not a meritorious cause of the grace granted me, but a certain occasion. [[1:14|Now the grace of our Lord hath abounded exceedingly|Superabundavit autem gratia Domini nostri]] of our Lord Jesus Christ in me, [[1:14|with faith and love|cum fide et dilectione]], that is, faith and love also, [[1:14|which is in Christ Jesus|quæ est in Christo Jesu]] as in cause and object, were abundantly infused into me: as I said elsewhere, [[Rom 5:20|where sin abounded, grace did more abound|Ubi abundavit iniquitas, superabundavit et gratia]].

paras.t: Consequenter ponit rationem cur gratia Dei abundavit in se, imo in omnibus iniquis conversis. Fidelis, id est verax fideliterque credendus, sermo, et omni acceptione dignus, id est maxime acceptabilis, gratus et amplectendus, qui sequitur: quia, id est quod, Christus Jesus venit per humanæ naturæ assumptionem in hunc mundum: juxta illud Baruch. Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est. Verbum enim caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Peccatores salvos facere, id est ad salvandum et liberandum iniquos, juxta illud Joannis: Non misit Deus Filium suum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum. Unde et ipse testatur: Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat; itemque. Non venit vocare justos, sed peccatores ad pœnitentiam. Quorum primus, id est præcipuus, ego sum, propter magnitudinem peccatorum meorum: non tamen simpliciter primus seu maximus, sed secundum aliquam considerationem, videlicet in quantum peccata mea certius scio et gravius pondero quam aliorum.
paras.en: Next he gives the reason why God's grace abounded in him, indeed in all the wicked who are converted. [[1:15|A faithful|Fidelis]], that is, true and to be faithfully believed, [[1:15|saying, and worthy of all acceptation|sermo, et omni acceptione dignus]], that is, supremely acceptable, welcome and to be embraced, the one that follows: [[1:15|that Christ Jesus came|quia, id est quod, Christus Jesus venit]] (*quia*, that is, *quod*, “that”), by assuming human nature, [[1:15|into the world|in hunc mundum]]: according to that of Baruch: [[Bar 3:38|Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est]]. [[John 1:14|And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us|Verbum enim caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis]]. [[1:15|to save sinners|Peccatores salvos facere]], that is, to save and deliver the wicked, according to that of John: [[John 3:17|For God sent not his Son into the world, to judge the world: but that the world may be saved by him|Non misit Deus Filium suum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum]]. Hence He Himself testifies: [[Luke 19:10|For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost|Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]]; and again: [[Matt 9:13|For I am not come to call the just, but sinners|Non venit vocare justos, sed peccatores]], to penance. [[1:15|of whom I am the chief|quorum primus ego sum]], that is, the foremost, because of the greatness of my sins: not, however, simply the first or greatest, but under a certain consideration, namely inasmuch as I know my own sins more surely and weigh them more heavily than those of others.

paras.t: Sed ideo misericordiam consecutus sum, ut in me, id est in mei piissima conversione et salvatione, primum, id est principaliter, ostenderet Christus Jesus omnem, id est perfectam, patientiam, id est longanimitatem et mansuetudinem suam, ad informationem eorum qui credituri sunt illi in vitam æternam, id est, ut omnes futuri fideles propter æternam vitam credituri, discant in me divinæ pietatis abyssum, quatenus nunquam desperent, considerantes me maximum peccatorem, in apostolum præelectum. Hæc est alia et major ac verior causa propter quam Deus misertus est Pauli, videlicet, ut poneret eum exemplum spei cunctis credentibus.
paras.en: [[1:16|But for this cause have I obtained mercy: that in me|Sed ideo misericordiam consecutus sum, ut in me]], that is, in my most loving conversion and salvation, [[1:16|first|primum]], that is, principally, [[1:16|Christ Jesus might shew forth all|ostenderet Christus Jesus omnem]], that is, perfect, [[1:16|patience|patientiam]], that is, His long-suffering and mildness, [[1:16|for the information of them that shall believe in him unto life everlasting|ad informationem eorum qui credituri sunt illi in vitam æternam]]: that is, so that all future faithful who are to believe for the sake of eternal life may learn in me the abyss of divine mercy, and so never despair, considering me, the greatest sinner, chosen beforehand to be an apostle. This is another, greater and truer cause why God had mercy on Paul: namely, to set him as an example of hope to all believers.

paras.t: Pro tantis igitur beneficiis gratias ago et dico: Regi autem sæculorum, id est Deo uni et trino, omnium generationum et temporum principi, omnia gubernanti, immortali, id est penitus invariabili, sicut et Jacobus loquitur: Apud quem non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio; invisibili, quia nec oculo corporali, nec intellectuali perfecte et comprehensive videtur, id est omnino incomprehensibili, sicut apud Joannem habetur: Deum nemo vidit unquam. Quæ enim sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus ejus. Soli Deo, id est Regi huic, qui solus est Deus, sit honor latriæ, id est summæ exhibitio reverentiæ, et gloria, id est beatitudo in se ipso; vel, Gloria, id est nominis sui clarificatio in cordibus hominum cum debita laude; in sæcula sæculorum, id est sine fine. Amen.
paras.en: For such great benefits, therefore, I give thanks and say: [[1:17|Now to the king of ages|Regi autem sæculorum]], that is, to God one and three, prince of all generations and times, governing all things, [[1:17|immortal|immortali]], that is, wholly unchangeable, as James also says: [[Jas 1:17|with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration|Apud quem non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio]]; [[1:17|invisible|invisibili]], because He is seen perfectly and comprehensively neither by the bodily eye nor by the intellectual, that is, wholly incomprehensible, as we have in John: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]]. [[1 Cor 2:11|the things also that are of God, no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God|Quæ enim sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus ejus]]. [[1:17|the only God|Soli Deo]], that is, to this King who alone is God, be [[1:17|honour|honor]] of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], that is, the showing of supreme reverence, [[1:17|and glory|et gloria]], that is, beatitude in Himself; or, glory, that is, the glorifying of His name in the hearts of men with due praise; [[1:17|for ever and ever|in sæcula sæculorum]], that is, without end. [[1:17|Amen|Amen]].

paras.t: Post divinorum beneficiorum recordationem, et humilitatis propriæ professionem ac devotissimam gratiarum actionem, docet Apostolus Timotheum quomodo in regimine gregis sui se habeat. Hoc præceptum quod subjungo, commendo tibi, fili Timothee, implendum secundum præcedentes in te prophetias, id est secundum revelationes propheticas mihi de te factas, antequam a me episcopus crearis: hoc est, sic impleas istud præceptum quemadmodum mihi Spiritus Sanctus revelavit de te priusquam te ordinarem episcopum. Præceptum autem est hoc: ut milites, id est, pugnando exerceas, in illis prophetiis adimplendis, bonam militiam, id est fructuosam exercitationem, resistendo falsis doctoribus, et veritatem prædicando, ac populum tuum regendo, sicut revelatum est mihi te operaturum, habens fidem plenam, et bonam conscientiam de nullo vitio sibi consciam.
paras.en: After recalling God's benefits, professing his own humility and giving most devout thanks, the Apostle teaches Timothy how to conduct himself in ruling his flock. [[1:18|This precept|Hoc præceptum]], which I add, [[1:18|I commend to thee, O son Timothy|commendo tibi, fili Timothee]], to be fulfilled [[1:18|according to the prophecies going before on thee|secundum præcedentes in te prophetias]], that is, according to the prophetic revelations made to me about thee before thou wast made bishop by me: that is, fulfil this precept as the Holy Ghost revealed to me concerning thee before I ordained thee bishop. And the precept is this: [[1:18|that thou war|ut milites]], that is, exercise by fighting, [[1:18|in them|in illis]], in fulfilling those prophecies, [[1:18|a good warfare|bonam militiam]], that is, a fruitful exercise, by resisting false teachers, preaching the truth and ruling thy people, as it was revealed to me thou wouldst do, [[1:19|Having faith|habens fidem]] full, [[1:19|and a good conscience|et bonam conscientiam]], conscious to itself of no vice.

paras.t: Quam conscientiam bonam quidam repellentes, id est peccando perdentes, circa fidem naufragaverunt, id est, in his quæ fidei sunt, erraverunt, et in profundum erroris submersi sunt. Ex quibus, id est de quorum numero, est Hymenæus et Alexander, quos tradidi Satanæ, id est excommunicavi, et excommunicatos exposui potestati diaboli, ut eos corporaliter vexet, donec resipiscant, ut discant per experientiam pœnarum suarum, non blasphemare: quemadmodum scriptum est, Sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui. Sicque traditio ista finaliter intendebat in emendationem ipsorum. Tantæ demum potestatis, ut dictum est, erat Apostolus, ut recedentes a fide solo verbo daret diabolo: qui nil potest nisi a Deo et Sanctis permissus. Unde traditio hæc, fuit prolatio sententiæ ab ore Apostoli contra eos: qua dæmon percepta, mox traditos apprehendit, et tribulavit per intervalla; imo interim etiam occidit corrigi non volentes.
paras.en: [[1:19|which some rejecting|quam quidam repellentes]], which good conscience, that is, losing it by sinning, [[1:19|have made shipwreck concerning the faith|circa fidem naufragaverunt]], that is, have erred in matters of faith and are sunk in the depth of error. [[1:20|Of whom|Ex quibus]], that is, of whose number, [[1:20|is Hymeneus and Alexander, whom I have delivered up to Satan|est Hymenæus et Alexander, quos tradidi Satanæ]], that is, I excommunicated them, and exposed them, excommunicated, to the power of the devil[[1 Cor 5:5||]], that he might afflict them bodily until they come to their senses, [[1:20|that they may learn|ut discant]] by experience of their punishments, [[1:20|not to blaspheme|non blasphemare]]: as it is written, [[Is 28:19|vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear|Sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui]]. And so this delivering up aimed finally at their amendment. So great, then, as has been said, was the Apostle's power, that by a word alone he could give over to the devil those who departed from the faith: the devil, who can do nothing unless permitted by God and the saints. Hence this delivering up was the pronouncing of sentence against them from the Apostle's mouth; which the demon perceiving, at once seized those delivered up and troubled them at intervals; indeed meanwhile he even slew those who would not be corrected.

2.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI SECUNDI : OBSECRO IGITUR PRIMO OMNIUM FIERI OBSECRATIONES.
2.title_en: Exposition of the second chapter: I desire therefore, first of all, that supplications be made.

paras.t: SECUNDUM doctores catholicos, in exordio hujus capituli, non solum Timotheo, sed universæ Ecclesiæ præscribit Apostolus formam celebrandi, atque pro omnibus supplicandi. Primo igitur Glossa exponit hunc locum, quantum ad Missæ officium, ut sit sensus: Obsecro igitur primo omnium, id est ante cetera, fieri obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes, gratiarum actiones. Obsecrationes dicuntur, quæ in Missa ante consecrationem proferuntur; orationes, quæ dicuntur in consecratione; postulationes vero, quæ post consecrationem, ut est episcopalis benedictio, vel dum aliquid ex debito petitur; gratiarum actiones autem, quæ dicuntur post sumptionem in fine officii. Secundo exponit, quantum ad officium orandi communiter. Sicque obsecrationes vocantur, quæ pro rebus difficilibus Domino offeruntur, ut est justificatio impii, suscitatio mortui: quamvis cuncta sint Deo æque facilia, cui non est difficile omne verbum, ut dicitur apud Jeremiam. Orationes dicuntur, dum conversis petuntur virtutes; postulationes vero, dum justis gloria sempiterna imprecatur. Gratiarum actiones, sunt hymni Deo oblati pro beneficiis ejus.
paras.en: According to the Catholic doctors, at the opening of this chapter the Apostle prescribes, not to Timothy alone but to the whole Church, the form of celebrating and of making supplication for all. First, then, the Gloss expounds this place with regard to the office of the Mass, so that the sense is: [[2:1|I desire therefore, first of all|Obsecro igitur primo omnium]], that is, before all else, [[2:1|that supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made|fieri obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes, gratiarum actiones]] [Denis's Latin words are *obsecrationes*, *orationes*, *postulationes* (literally "requests") and *gratiarum actiones*]. Supplications are the name for those uttered in the Mass before the consecration; prayers, those said at the consecration; intercessions, those after the consecration, such as the bishop's blessing, or when something is asked as owed; and thanksgivings, those said after the communion, at the end of the office. Secondly, it expounds it with regard to the office of praying in general. And so supplications is the name for those offered to the Lord for difficult things, such as the justification of the wicked or the raising of the dead: although all things are equally easy to God, for, as is said in Jeremias, to him [[Jer 32:17|no word shall be hard|non est difficile omne verbum]][[Jer 32:27||]] [*verbum*, "word", stands here, as often in Scripture, for a thing done]. Prayers is the name when virtues are asked for the converted; intercessions, when everlasting glory is called down upon the just. Thanksgivings are hymns offered to God for his benefits.

paras.t: Quidam distinguunt hæc quattuor ita: nam ad actum precationis tria exiguntur. Primum, est accessus precantis ad Deum: quod fit per orationem, quæ secundum Damascenum est ascensus mentis ad Deum. Et quantum ad hoc, dicit Apostolus: Obsecro fieri orationes. Secundum, est proponere coram Deo quod petitur: quod fit dupliciter, scilicet, in communi, sicut quum dicimus: Domine, adsis mihi, vel, adjuva me; et in speciali, ut quum dicimus: Domine, da mihi caritatis fervorem. Primo modo vocatur petitio, secundo, postulatio. Tertium, quod ad actum precationis exigitur, est id per quod fit exaudibilis: quod est duplex. Unum enim est ex parte Dei, videlicet sanctitas ejus, vel aliquid sanctificatum ab eo, sicut quum dicimus: Per tuam bonitatem, vel, tuam Incarnationem, libera nos. Aliud est ex parte orantis, videlicet gratitudo seu gratiarum actio de bonis collatis, per quam dignificatur homo ad percipienda dona majora. Ad quorum primum pertinent obsecrationes, ad secundum gratiarum actiones.
paras.en: Some distinguish these four thus. For three things are required for the act of praying. The first is the approach of the one who prays to God, which is made by prayer, which according to Damascene is the ascent of the mind to God. And as to this the Apostle says: [[2:1|I desire|Obsecro fieri]] [[2:1|prayers|orationes]] be made. The second is to set forth before God what is asked, which is done in two ways: in general, as when we say, Lord, be with me, or, Help me; and in particular, as when we say, Lord, give me the fervour of charity. In the first way it is called a petition, in the second a request [*postulatio*: the word rendered "intercessions" in the Douay-Rheims]. The third thing required for the act of praying is that by which it becomes worthy to be heard, and this is twofold. One is on God's side, namely his holiness, or something sanctified by him, as when we say: By thy goodness, or, By thy Incarnation, deliver us. The other is on the side of the one who prays, namely gratitude, or thanksgiving for good things bestowed, by which a man is made worthy to receive greater gifts. To the first of these belong supplications [*obsecrationes*: entreaties made by appeal to something holy, *per sacra*], to the second thanksgivings.

paras.t: Has igitur orationis species obsecro fieri, id est a fidelibus, præsertim a sacerdotibus, Deo offerri, pro omnibus hominibus fidelibus et infidelibus, amicis et inimicis, notis et ignotis, præcipue tamen pro regibus, et omnibus qui in sublimitate sunt constituti, id est prælatis atque principibus, ex quorum bono regimine, aliorum salus pro magna parte dependet, juxta illud: Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus; et qualis est rector civitatis, tales et inhabitantes in ea. His etiam majus onus incumbit, majusque periculum imminet: quia judicium gravissimum fiet in his qui præsunt. Subditi quoque specialiter obligantur orare pro eis. Ut quietam ab exterioribus perturbationibus, et tranquillam, id est intus pacificam, vitam agamus in omni pietate animæ, et castitate corporis, sumendo castitatem pro continentia; vel, In omni pietate, quantum ad alios, et castitate, id est temperantia, quantum ad nos ipsos.
paras.en: These kinds of prayer, then, [[2:1|I desire|obsecro]] [[2:1|be made|fieri]], that is, offered to God by the faithful, and above all by priests, [[2:1|for all men|pro omnibus hominibus]], faithful and unbelievers, friends and enemies, known and unknown; but chiefly [[2:2|for kings and for all that are in high station|pro regibus, et omnibus qui in sublimitate sunt constituti]], that is, for prelates and princes, on whose good government the salvation of others in great part depends, according to that saying: [[Ecclus 10:2|As the judge of the people is himself, so also are his ministers: and what manner of man the ruler of a city is, such also are they that dwell therein.|Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus; et qualis est rector civitatis, tales et inhabitantes in ea]] Upon them, too, lies a heavier burden, and over them hangs a greater danger, since a most severe judgment shall be passed on those that rule [compare Wis 6:6]. Subjects, moreover, are especially bound to pray for them. [[2:2|That we may lead a quiet|Ut quietam]] (quiet from outward disturbances) [[2:2|and a peaceable|et tranquillam]] (that is, at peace within) [[2:2|life|vitam agamus]] [[2:2|in all piety|in omni pietate]] of soul [[2:2|and chastity|et castitate]] of body, taking chastity for continence; or else, [[2:2|in all piety|In omni pietate]] as regards others, [[2:2|and chastity|et castitate]], that is, temperance, as regards ourselves.

paras.t: Hoc enim, id est sic orare pro omnibus, bonum est et acceptum, id est virtuosum, meritorium et placitum, coram Salvatore nostro Deo, qui omnes homines vult salvos fieri, et ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Hoc idem alibi sæpe testatur Scriptura. Scriptum est namque: Non est voluntas ante Patrem vestrum ut pereat unus ex pusillis istis; et iterum, Patienter agit Dominus propter vos, nolens aliquem perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reverti. Et rursus per Prophetam: Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii, dicit Dominus, et non ut convertatur a viis suis, et vivat? Imo, in tantum vult et quasi desiderat Deus nostram salutem, ut per alium Prophetam populo impio dicat: Utinam attendisses mandata mea. — Sed difficultas est, quomodo sint hæc intelligenda, propter auctoritates Scripturæ quæ videntur oppositum velle. Nam alibi dicit Apostolus: Voluntati ejus quis resistit? Et per Isaiam Dominus perhibet: Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet. Et Psalmista: Omnia, inquit, quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit. Si ergo vult omnes salvari, ergo omnes salvarentur.
paras.en: [[2:3|For this|Hoc enim]], that is, to pray thus for all, [[2:3|is good and acceptable|bonum est et acceptum]], that is, virtuous, meritorious and pleasing, [[2:3|in the sight of God our Saviour|coram Salvatore nostro Deo]], [[2:4|Who will have all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.|qui omnes homines vult salvos fieri, et ad agnitionem veritatis venire]] Scripture often bears witness to this same thing elsewhere. For it is written: [[Matt 18:14|it is not the will of your Father|Non est voluntas ante Patrem vestrum]] [[Matt 18:14|that one of these little ones should perish|ut pereat unus ex pusillis istis]]; and again, the Lord [[2 Pet 3:9|dealeth patiently for your sake, not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance|Patienter agit Dominus propter vos, nolens aliquem perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reverti]]. And again, by the Prophet: [[Ezech 18:23|Is it my will that a sinner should die, saith the Lord God, and not that he should be converted from his ways, and live?|Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii, dicit Dominus, et non ut convertatur a viis suis, et vivat?]] Nay, so much does God will and, as it were, long for our salvation that by another Prophet he says to a wicked people: [[Is 48:18|O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments|Utinam attendisses mandata mea]]. But there is a difficulty as to how these things are to be understood, because of the authorities of Scripture that seem to mean the opposite. For elsewhere the Apostle says: [[Rom 9:19|who resisteth his will?|Voluntati ejus quis resistit?]] And by Isaias the Lord declares: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done|Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 134:6|Whatsoever|Omnia]], he says, [[Ps 134:6|the Lord pleased he hath done|quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit]]. If, then, he wills all to be saved, all would therefore be saved.

paras.t: Ad hoc multipliciter respondetur: Primo, quod Deus vult omnes salvari quantum in se est, ita ut ex parte ejus non sit defectus, neminemque ad se venientem repellat, et singulis gratiam dare paratus sit, si fecerint quod in se est. Secundo, intelligitur cum distributione accommoda seu impletione, ut sit sensus: Vult omnes salvos fieri, id est, omnes qui salvantur, vult salvos fieri. Nemo enim salvatur nisi Deo volente. Tertio, intelligitur cum distributione pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum. De omni enim statu et genere hominum vult quosdam salvari. Hæc tamen responsio non videtur satisfacere auctoritati qua dictum est, quod non sit voluntas Patris ut pereat unus ex pusillis istis. Quarto, intelligitur de voluntate signi. Nam Deus consulit, hortatur, et jubet, ut omnes bene se habeant. Quinta responsio, quæ melior est, et a Damasceno assignatur, est quod Deus vult omnes salvari voluntate antecedente, non autem voluntate consequente: quæ duplex voluntas in Deo, sola ratione distinguitur. Dicitur enim voluntas antecedens, qua quis aliquid vult secundum considerationem communem et absolutam rei quam vult; consequens vero, qua vult aliquid consideratis particularibus circumstantiis atque conditionibus ejus. Primo modo vult rex omnes suos subjectos vivere, in quantum videlicet considerat eos ut cives et membra regni sui; secundo modo vult quosdam eorum perire, in quantum sunt bono communi contrarii, vel enormiter scelerati. Simili modo vult Deus omnes homines salvari, voluntate antecedente, videlicet considerati eis ut sunt rationalis naturæ ad Dei imaginem factæ, beatitudinisque capaces; sed considerando nonnullos secundum actus et circumstantias suas particulares, non vult eos salvari, sed damnari: quod pertinet ad voluntatem consequentem. Verum, ut ait Thomas, voluntas fertur in rem secundum quod res in se realiter exsistit. Ideo quod aliquis vult voluntate antecedente, non vult simpliciter, sed secundum quid; quod vero vult voluntate consequente, vult simpliciter et perfecte. Ideo omnes salvantur quos vult Deus salvari, loquendo de voluntate Dei æterna simpliciter dicta.
paras.en: To this many answers are given. First, that God wills all to be saved as far as lies in him, so that there is no failing on his part; he repels no one who comes to him[[John 6:37||]], and is ready to give grace to each, if they do what lies in them. Secondly, it is understood with a fitting distribution, or restriction [that is, "all" is taken to mean "all of a certain number"], so that the sense is: He wills all to be saved, that is, all who are saved he wills to be saved; for no one is saved unless God wills it. Thirdly, it is understood with a distribution over the kinds of individuals, not over the individuals of each kind [that is, some men of every kind, not every man of every kind]: for of every state and kind of men he wills some to be saved. This answer, however, does not seem to satisfy the authority in which it is said that it is not the will of the Father [[Matt 18:14|that one of these little ones should perish|ut pereat unus ex pusillis istis]]. Fourthly, it is understood of the will of sign [that is, God's will as shown outwardly by signs, such as counsel and command, as distinct from his will of good pleasure]: for God counsels, exhorts and commands that all should live well. The fifth answer, which is the better one and is given by Damascene, is that God wills all to be saved by his antecedent will, but not by his consequent will: and this twofold will in God is distinguished by reason alone. For that is called antecedent will by which one wills something according to a general and absolute consideration of the thing willed; but consequent, that by which one wills something when its particular circumstances and conditions have been considered. In the first way a king wills all his subjects to live, inasmuch as he considers them as citizens and members of his kingdom; in the second way he wills some of them to perish, inasmuch as they are hostile to the common good, or monstrously wicked. In like manner God wills all men to be saved by his antecedent will, that is, considering them as being of a rational nature made to the image of God and capable of beatitude; but considering some according to their particular acts and circumstances, he does not will them to be saved, but to be damned: and this belongs to the consequent will. But, as Thomas says, the will is borne toward a thing according as the thing really exists in itself. Therefore what one wills by antecedent will, he does not will absolutely, but only in a certain respect; but what he wills by consequent will, he wills absolutely and perfectly. Therefore all are saved whom God wills to be saved, speaking of God's eternal will taken absolutely.

paras.t: Quod ergo vult Deus omnes salvari his modis, declarat Apostolus. Unus enim Deus est, utpote in essentia simplex, et in Personis trinus, qui est Trinitas superbenedicta, unus verus simplicissimus Deus; unus est et mediator, id est reconciliator et sequester, Dei Trinitatis et hominum, homo Christus Jesus, cum utroque extremo conveniens: cum Deo, secundum naturam divinam; et cum hominibus, secundum assumptam humanitatem. Estque mediator Dei ac hominum, proprie loquendo, nec ut Deus, neque ut homo, sed ut Deus homo, seu ut Deus incarnatus. Sic quippe competit ei et satisfacere seu reconciliare, et idoneitas vel efficacia reconciliandi: quorum primum convenit ei ratione assumptæ naturæ; secundum vero, ratione Deitatis unitæ, ex qua opera et pœnæ Christi hominis infinitam quodammodo dignitatem et efficaciam sortiuntur, in tantum ut minima gutta sanguinis ejus, fuisset sufficientissima ad totius humani generis liberationem. Qui Christus dedit, id est, sponte et caritative obtulit, redemptionem, id est in causam et pretium nostræ redemptionis, semetipsum pro omnibus, quantum ad sufficientiam.
paras.en: That God, then, wills all to be saved in these ways, the Apostle makes plain. [[2:5|For there is one God|Unus enim Deus est]], being simple in essence and three in Persons, who is the Trinity blessed above all, [[2:5|one|unus]] true and most simple God; [[2:5|and one mediator|unus est et mediator]], that is, reconciler and go-between, [[2:5|of God|Dei]] the Trinity [[2:5|and men|et hominum]], [[2:5|the man Christ Jesus|homo Christus Jesus]], who is at one with each extreme: with God according to the divine nature, and with men according to the humanity he assumed. And he is mediator of God and men, properly speaking, neither as God nor as man, but as God-man, or as God incarnate. For so it belongs to him both to make satisfaction, or to reconcile, and to have the fitness or power to reconcile: the first of which belongs to him by reason of the nature assumed, the second by reason of the Godhead united to it, from which the works and sufferings of Christ the man obtain a dignity and power in a manner infinite, so much so that the least drop of his blood would have been more than enough for the deliverance of the whole human race. [[2:6|Who|Qui]], Christ, [[2:6|gave|dedit]], that is, freely and out of charity offered, [[2:6|himself|semetipsum]] [[2:6|a redemption|redemptionem]], that is, as the cause and price of our redemption, [[2:6|for all|pro omnibus]], as regards sufficiency [that is, his death is enough to redeem all men, though not all receive its fruit].

paras.t: Cujus testimonium, id est assertio seu prædicatio, utpote testimonium quod vel Prophetæ præbuerunt de Christo venturo, vel Apostoli de ipso jam passo et glorificato, temporibus suis, id est diebus a Deo præordinatis, confirmatum est, id est impletum et verificatum, atque per signa divina probatum, videlicet in die sancto Pentecostes adveniente Spiritu Sancto, et Apostolis Christi resurrectionem prædicantibus, ac diversa miracula operantibus. Unde scriptum est: Illi profecti prædicaverunt ubique, Domino cooperante, et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis. In quo, id est ad cujus testimonii perhibitionem seu prædicationem, positus, id est divinitus institutus et factus, sum ego prædicator et apostolus. Veritatem dico in Christo, et non mentior ista dicendo, qui sum doctor gentium in fide catholica et veritate evangelicæ legis.
paras.en: Of which the [[2:6|testimony|testimonium]], that is, the assertion or preaching (the testimony, namely, which either the Prophets gave of Christ to come, or the Apostles of him who had already suffered and been glorified), [[2:6|in due times|temporibus suis]], that is, in the days foreordained by God, was confirmed [these words, *confirmatum est*, are in Denis's text but not in the Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims], that is, fulfilled and verified, and proved by divine signs: namely, on the holy day of Pentecost[[Acts 2:1||]], when the Holy Ghost came[[Acts 2:4||]], and the Apostles preached the resurrection of Christ and worked divers miracles. Hence it is written: [[Mark 16:20|they going forth preached every where: the Lord working withal, and confirming the word with signs that followed|Illi profecti prædicaverunt ubique, Domino cooperante, et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis]]. [[2:7|Whereunto|In quo]], that is, for the bearing and preaching of which testimony, [[2:7|I am appointed|positus]], that is, divinely instituted and made, [[2:7|a preacher and an apostle|sum ego prædicator et apostolus]]. [[2:7|I say the truth|Veritatem dico]] in Christ, and [[2:7|I lie not|non mentior]] in saying these things, I who am [[2:7|a doctor of the Gentiles|doctor gentium]] in the Catholic [[2:7|faith|fide]] and in the [[2:7|truth|veritate]] of the gospel law.

paras.t: Insuper docet Apostolus modum orandi in speciali: primo, quantum ad viros. Volo ergo, id est, quoniam doctor sum gentium, volo viros orare, id est decentia petere a Deo, in omni loco, opportunitate adepta, et non solum in ecclesia materiali; levantes puras manus, id est sancta desideria cum corporalium manuum extensione ad Deum, pro devotione ardentiori excitanda: si tamen fieri possit secrete. Coram aliis namque singularitas est vitanda. Multum autem confert corporalium manuum elevatio ad superna, pro interiori elevatione provocanda. Propter quod per Prophetam dicitur: Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Dominum in cælos; et rursus apud alium: In nomine tuo levabo manus meas: itemque, Elevatio manuum mearum sacrificium vespertinum. Sine ira in proximum, id est sine appetitu vindictæ et animæ commotione. Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur: Homo homini servat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam? Quis exorabit pro peccatis illius? Et disceptatione, id est hæsitatione quantum ad Deum, non dubitantes de exauditione, dummodo orent sicut oportet, videlicet, salubriter, perseveranter, et pro se ipsis. Cum plena ergo fiducia est orandum. Quis enim invocavit Deum, et despexit eum? Ideo per Jacobum dicitur: Postulet in fide nihil hæsitans.
paras.en: Further, the Apostle teaches the manner of praying in particular: first, as regards men. [[2:8|I will therefore|Volo ergo]], that is, since I am the doctor of the Gentiles, I will [[2:8|that men pray|viros orare]], that is, ask of God what is fitting, [[2:8|in every place|in omni loco]], when the opportunity offers, and not only in the material church; [[2:8|lifting up pure hands|levantes puras manus]], that is, holy desires, together with the stretching out of the bodily hands to God, to stir up a more ardent devotion: provided, however, that it can be done in secret, for before others singularity is to be avoided. And the lifting up of the bodily hands to things above does much to call forth the inward lifting up. For which reason it is said by the Prophet: [[Lam 3:41|Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens|Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Dominum in cælos]]; and again in another: [[Ps 62:5|in thy name I will lift up my hands|In nomine tuo levabo manus meas]]; and likewise: [[Ps 140:2|the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice|Elevatio manuum mearum sacrificium vespertinum]]. [[2:8|Without anger|Sine ira]] toward one's neighbour, that is, without desire of revenge or disturbance of soul. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 28:3|Man to man reserveth anger, and doth he seek remedy of God?|Homo homini servat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam?]] [[Ecclus 28:5|who shall obtain pardon for his sins?|Quis exorabit pro peccatis illius?]] [[2:8|And contention|Et disceptatione]] [Denis takes *disceptatio*, "dispute", as inward debate, that is, doubting], that is, without hesitation toward God, not doubting that they will be heard, provided they pray as they ought, namely, for what is good for salvation, perseveringly, and for themselves [the conditions under which, according to the theologians, prayer is infallibly heard]. We must pray, then, with full confidence. For [[Ecclus 2:12|who hath called upon him, and he despised him?|Quis enim invocavit Deum, et despexit eum?]] Therefore it is said by James: [[Jas 1:6|let him ask in faith, nothing wavering|Postulet in fide nihil hæsitans]].

paras.t: Similiter et mulieres volo orare, sicut de viris prædixi, cum manuum purarum levatione, sine ira et disceptatione, existentes in habitu ornato, id est veste decenti, non curiosa; cum verecundia: quæ est passio laudabilis, quum sit timor de re turpi, secundum Damascenum. Hinc scriptum est: Gratia super gratiam mulier sancta et pudorata et tacita. Et rursus: Fallax gratia et vana est pulchritudo; mulier timens Dominum, ipsa laudabitur. Et sobrietate, ne sint gulosæ. Ornantes se, non in tortis, id est crispatis, crinibus, aut auro, aut margaritis, vel veste pretiosa, sed quod decet mulieres, illo ornentur; illudque faciant, promittentes, id est firmiter proponentes, vel Deo voventes, vel foris veraciter ostendentes, pietatem, id est religiosam benignitatem seu christianam religionem et misericordiam, per opera bona, id est virtuose vivendo. Hoc et Petrus in prima sua docet Canonica: Mulierum non sit extrinsecus capillatura, aut circumdatio auri, aut indumenti vestimentorum cultus; sed qui absconditus cordis est homo, in incorruptibilitate quieti et modesti spiritus.
paras.en: [[2:9|In like manner, women also|Similiter et mulieres]]: I will that they too pray, as I said before of the men, [[2:8|lifting up pure hands, without anger and contention|cum manuum purarum levatione, sine ira et disceptatione]], being [[2:9|in decent apparel|in habitu ornato]], that is, in seemly dress, not elaborate; [[2:9|with modesty|cum verecundia]] [*verecundia*: shame, bashfulness], which is a praiseworthy passion, since it is fear of something shameful, according to Damascene. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 26:19|A holy and shamefaced woman is grace upon grace|Gratia super gratiam mulier sancta et pudorata]], and [[Ecclus 26:18|silent|et tacita]]. And again: [[Prov 31:30|Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: the woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.|Fallax gratia et vana est pulchritudo; mulier timens Dominum, ipsa laudabitur]] [[2:9|And sobriety|Et sobrietate]], so that they be not gluttonous. [[2:9|Adorning themselves|Ornantes se]], [[2:9|not with plaited|non in tortis]], that is, curled, [[2:9|hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly attire|crinibus, aut auro, aut margaritis, vel veste pretiosa]]; [[2:10|But, as it becometh women|sed quod decet mulieres]], with that let them be adorned; and let them do it [[2:10|professing|promittentes]] [literally "promising"], that is, firmly purposing, or vowing to God, or truly showing outwardly, [[2:10|godliness|pietatem]] [*pietas*, "piety"], that is, devout kindness, or the Christian religion and mercy, [[2:10|with good works|per opera bona]], that is, by living virtuously. Peter too teaches this in his first canonical Epistle: Of women, [[1 Pet 3:3|let it not be the outward plaiting of the hair, or the wearing of gold, or the putting on of apparel|non sit extrinsecus capillatura, aut circumdatio auri, aut indumenti vestimentorum cultus]]; [[1 Pet 3:4|But the hidden man of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and a meek spirit|sed qui absconditus cordis est homo, in incorruptibilitate quieti et modesti spiritus]].

paras.t: Mulier in silentio discat, id est, silenter instruentem seu prædicantem advertat, præsertim in ecclesia, cum omni subjectione interiori ac exteriori, id est cum perfecta humiliatione. Docere autem viros in publico seu in ecclesia mulieri non permitto: quia communiter ratio debilis est in feminis, suntque nimis loquaces, et ad vanitatem proclives; sermo quoque earum luxuriam potius incitat sæpe, quam devotionem, juxta illud, Colloquium mulieris quasi ignis exardescit. Verumtamen mulieres in suis conventibus seu domibus docere possunt personas sibi subjectas. Neque permitto mulieri dominari in virum, id est proprium maritum, sed esse in silentio, quum sint pronæ ad vitia locutionis.
paras.en: [[2:11|Let the woman learn in silence|Mulier in silentio discat]], that is, let her silently attend to the one instructing or preaching, especially in church, [[2:11|with all subjection|cum omni subjectione]], inward and outward, that is, with perfect humility. [[2:12|But I suffer not a woman|mulieri non permitto]] [[2:12|to teach|Docere autem]] men in public or in church: for reason is commonly weak in women, and they are too talkative and inclined to vanity; their speech, too, often stirs up lust rather than devotion, according to that saying: a woman's [[Ecclus 9:11|conversation burneth as fire|Colloquium mulieris quasi ignis exardescit]]. Women may nevertheless teach those subject to them in their own convents or houses. [[2:12|Nor|Neque]] do I suffer a woman [[2:12|to use authority over the man|dominari in virum]], that is, over her own husband, [[2:12|but to be in silence|sed esse in silentio]], since they are prone to the faults of the tongue.

paras.t: Ideo autem debet esse viro subjecta: Adam enim primus formatus est, id est a Deo ante mulierem creatus, deinde Eva de latere viri. Et Adam non est seductus a serpente, credendo vera esse quæ dixerat serpens, videlicet, Quacumque die comederitis, etc., eritis sicut dii; mulier autem seducta in prævaricatione fuit, id est decepta promissione serpentis, dicentis, Nequaquam moriemini, sed eritis sicut dii: in tantum ut de prohibito fructu comederit. Unde Adam interrogatus a Deo, non dixit, Mulier seduxit me; sed, Dedit mihi, et comedi. Illa vero, Serpens, inquit, decepit me, et comedi. Adam enim multo sapientior atque perfectior erat uxore: unde nequaquam putavit verba Dei esse mendosa; seductus tamen fuit in hoc, quod propter amorem conjugis manducavit de vetito fructu, nec putavit transgressionem suam tam graviter puniendam.
paras.en: And she ought to be subject to her husband for this reason: [[2:13|For Adam was first formed|Adam enim primus formatus est]], that is, created by God before the woman[[Gen 2:7||]]; [[2:13|then Eve|deinde Eva]], from the side of the man[[Gen 2:21||]]. [[2:14|And Adam was not seduced|Et Adam non est seductus]] by the serpent, so as to believe true what the serpent had said, namely: [[Gen 3:5|in what day soever you shall eat|Quacumque die comederitis]], etc., [[Gen 3:5|you shall be as Gods|eritis sicut dii]]; [[2:14|but the woman, being seduced, was in the transgression|mulier autem seducta in prævaricatione fuit]], that is, she was deceived by the promise of the serpent, who said: [[Gen 3:4|No, you shall not die|Nequaquam moriemini]], but [[Gen 3:5|you shall be as Gods|eritis sicut dii]]; so much so that she ate of the forbidden fruit. Hence Adam, when questioned by God, did not say, The woman seduced me, but: She [[Gen 3:12|gave me|Dedit mihi]], [[Gen 3:12|and I did eat|et comedi]]. But she: [[Gen 3:13|The serpent|Serpens]], she says, [[Gen 3:13|deceived me, and I did eat|decepit me, et comedi]]. For Adam was far wiser and more perfect than his wife, and so he by no means thought the words of God false; yet he was seduced in this, that for love of his wife he ate of the forbidden fruit, and did not think his transgression would be punished so severely.

paras.t: Salvabitur autem, id est, salutis augmentum merebitur et sortietur mulier, per filiorum generationem corporalem vel spiritualem. Nam actus matrimonii meritorius est, si cum debitis circumstantiis exerceatur, videlicet, propter prolem divino cultui deputandam. Spiritualis quoque generatio, quæ est instructio, correctio et educatio in virtutibus, multum meritoria est matri. Si permanserit in fide catholica et dilectione spirituali, ne amor carnalis in ea prævaleat, et sanctificatione, id est sancta conversatione, præsertim vitando alterius viri pollutionem, cum sobrietate, temperanter vivendo. Immoderatio enim cibi ac potus, plurima vitia parit in feminis.
paras.en: [[2:15|Yet she shall be saved|Salvabitur autem]], that is, the woman shall merit and obtain an increase of salvation, [[2:15|through child bearing|per filiorum generationem]], bodily or spiritual. For the act of marriage is meritorious if it is performed with the due circumstances, namely, for the sake of offspring to be devoted to the worship of God. The spiritual bearing of children, too, which is their instruction, correction and upbringing in the virtues, is very meritorious for the mother. [[2:15|If she continue in faith|Si permanserit in fide]], the Catholic faith, [[2:15|and love|et dilectione]], spiritual love, lest carnal love prevail in her, [[2:15|and sanctification|et sanctificatione]], that is, holy conduct, above all by shunning defilement with another man, [[2:15|with sobriety|cum sobrietate]], by living temperately. For immoderation in food and drink breeds very many vices in women.

3.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI TERTII : FIDELIS SERMO : SI QUIS EPISCOPATUM DESIDERAT, ETC.
3.title_en: Exposition of the third chapter: A faithful saying: if a man desire the office of a bishop, etc.

paras.t: Consequenter Apostolus instruit Timotheum de ordinatione ministrorum Ecclesiæ. Fidelis, id est verus et gratus, est sermo qui subditur, scilicet: Si quis episcopatum desiderat, id est, episcopus fieri cupit, bonum opus, id est sanctum officium, desiderat; sed non bene desiderat. Non enim licere videtur ad episcopatum anhelare, nisi forte ex speciali inspiratione Spiritus Sancti. Quamvis enim episcopatus sit dignitas magna, habet tamen summum laborem et maximam sollicitudinem sibi annexam, ita ut potius appelletur opus quam dignitas. Et si quis episcopatum licite cupit, non propter dignitatem, sed propter administrationem eum cupit, optans prodesse, non præesse. Denique nomen episcopi proprie sumptum, significat opus, non dignitatem. Dicitur enim, ab ἐπί, quod est supra, et σκοπός, intentio, quasi saluti gregis superintendens. Quidam probabiliter asserunt hoc loco per episcopatum intelligi sacerdotium. Nam de diaconis statim subjungitur. Non autem apparet quod Apostolus de sacerdotio conticuisset, tantumque ordinem transiliisset, nisi in nomine episcopatus includeretur.
paras.en: Next the Apostle instructs Timothy on the ordering of the ministers of the Church. [[3:1|A faithful|Fidelis]], that is, true and welcome, [[3:1|saying|est sermo]] is what follows, namely: [[3:1|If a man desire the office of a bishop|Si quis episcopatum desiderat]], that is, longs to become a bishop, [[3:1|he desireth good work|bonum opus]], that is, a holy office; but he does not desire well. For it does not seem lawful to aspire eagerly to the episcopate, unless perhaps by a special inspiration of the Holy Spirit. For although the episcopate is a great dignity, it has the greatest labour and the utmost solicitude joined to it, so that it is rather to be called a work than a dignity. And if anyone lawfully desires the episcopate, he desires it not for the dignity but for the administration, wishing to be of profit, not to preside [*prodesse, non præesse*: a play on the two words]. Indeed the name of bishop, taken properly, signifies a work, not a dignity. For it is said from ἐπί, which is "over", and σκοπός, "intention", as one superintending the salvation of the flock. Some assert with probability that in this place the priesthood is understood by the episcopate. For he goes on at once to speak of deacons; and it does not appear that the Apostle would have passed over the priesthood in silence and leapt over so great an order, unless it were included in the name of the episcopate.

paras.t: Ne autem quispiam pronus sit ad episcopatum desiderandum, declarat Apostolus qualem oportet esse episcopum, quatenus episcopatum nemo affectet nisi virtutibus istis ornetur. Oportet ergo, si res digne et fructuose agatur, episcopatum jam creatum, vel eum qui ad episcopatum promovetur, sine crimine esse, id est sine magno, perseveranti seu notabili vitio, ne increpanti dicatur: Medice, cura te ipsum.
paras.en: But lest anyone be prone to desire the episcopate, the Apostle declares what manner of man a bishop must be, so that no one may aspire to the episcopate unless he is adorned with these virtues. [[3:2|It behoveth therefore|Oportet ergo]], if the thing is to be done worthily and fruitfully, [[3:2|a bishop|episcopatum]] [Denis's text reads *episcopatum*, "the episcopate", for the Vulgate's *episcopum*] already made, or him who is being promoted to the episcopate, [[3:2|to be blameless|sine crimine esse]] [Denis's text reads *sine crimine*, "without crime"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *irreprehensibilem*, "blameless"], that is, without great, persistent or notable vice, lest it be said to him in reproach: [[Luke 4:23|Physician, heal thyself|Medice, cura te ipsum]].

paras.t: Unius uxoris virum. Circa hoc Hieronymus et Augustinus dissentiunt. Hieronymus enim affirmat, quod oportet eum non habuisse nisi unam uxorem post Baptismum, ita quod non obest si ante Baptismum aliam habuit, eo quod Baptismus irregularitatem tollat. Augustinus tenet oppositum, quia Baptismus non sacramenta relaxat, sed crimina.
paras.en: [[3:2|the husband of one wife|Unius uxoris virum]]. On this Jerome and Augustine disagree. For Jerome affirms that he must not have had more than one wife after Baptism, so that it is no hindrance if he had another before Baptism, since Baptism takes away irregularity [that is, the canonical impediment to receiving holy orders]. Augustine holds the opposite, because Baptism does not loose sacraments, but crimes [that is, Baptism remits sins, but does not undo a marriage, which is a sacrament].

paras.t: Sobrium in victu, ne gravetur cor ejus crapula vel ebrietate. Unde in Levitico Dominus ait ministris Synagogæ, Aaroni scilicet et filiis ejus: Vinum et omne quod inebriare potest, non bibetis tu et filii tui, quando intrabitis in tabernaculum testimonii, ut habeatis scientiam discernendi inter sanctum et pollutum. Prudentem in agendis et dandis consiliis, pudicum in exteriori apparatu, honestum, ornatum probitate morum, hospitalem, alios (maxime pauperes) clementer hospitando, doctorem, id est eruditum et agilem ad docendum.
paras.en: [[3:2|sober|Sobrium]] in diet, lest his heart be overcharged with surfeiting or drunkenness[[Luke 21:34||]]. Hence in Leviticus the Lord says to the ministers of the Synagogue, that is, to Aaron and his sons: [[Lev 10:9|You shall not drink wine nor any thing that may make drunk, thou nor thy sons, when you enter into the tabernacle of the testimony|Vinum et omne quod inebriare potest, non bibetis tu et filii tui, quando intrabitis in tabernaculum testimonii]], [[Lev 10:10|that you may have knowledge to discern between holy and unholy|ut habeatis scientiam discernendi inter sanctum et pollutum]]. [[3:2|prudent|Prudentem]] in doing things and in giving counsel, [[3:2|chaste|pudicum]] in outward attire, honourable, [[3:2|of good behaviour|ornatum]] [*ornatum*, literally "adorned"], adorned with uprightness of conduct, [[3:2|given to hospitality|hospitalem]], receiving others (above all the poor) kindly as guests, [[3:2|a teacher|doctorem]], that is, learned and ready to teach.

paras.t: Non vinolentum, ne corpus ejus ad libidinem concitetur; non percussorem, id est bellicosum, vel ex impatientia verberantem, sed modestum, id est in omnibus ordinatum. Non litigiosum, ne verbis contendat. Honor enim est homini qui separat se a lite; et, Ubi zelus et contentio, ibi inconstantia et omne opus pravum. Non cupidum, ne propter munera pervertat judicium, vel acceptor sit personarum.
paras.en: [[3:3|Not given to wine|Non vinolentum]], lest his body be stirred up to lust; [[3:3|no striker|non percussorem]], that is, not quarrelsome in fighting, nor one who strikes out of impatience, [[3:3|but modest|sed modestum]], that is, ordered in all things. [[3:3|not quarrelsome|Non litigiosum]], lest he contend in words. For [[Prov 20:3|It is an honour for a man to separate himself from quarrels|Honor enim est homini qui separat se a lite]] [the margin gives Prov. xx, 1; the words are Prov 20:3]; and, [[Jas 3:16|where envying and contention is: there is inconstancy and every evil work|Ubi zelus et contentio, ibi inconstantia et omne opus pravum]]. [[3:3|not covetous|Non cupidum]], lest for gifts he pervert judgment, or be a respecter of persons.

paras.t: Suæ domui bene præpositum, id est propriam familiam digne regentem. Virtus namque et vitium familiæ, redundat in patremfamilias. Qualis enim rector, tales et subditi. Filios habentem subditos sibi et Deo in omni castitate, id est continentia, quæ omni Christiano necessaria est.
paras.en: [[3:4|One that ruleth well his own house|Suæ domui bene præpositum]], that is, governing his own household worthily. For the virtue and the vice of the household redound upon the father of the family. For as the ruler is, such also are the subjects[[Ecclus 10:2||]] [the margin gives Luc. x, 2, evidently for Eccli. x, 2, whose sense Denis gives loosely]. [[3:4|having his children in subjection|Filios habentem subditos]] to himself and to God, [[3:4|with all chastity|in omni castitate]], that is, continence, which is necessary to every Christian.

paras.t: Si quis autem domui suæ, id est domesticis, præesse nescit, quomodo Ecclesiæ Dei diligentiam habebit? id est, qualiter toti congregationi fidelium cum debita sollicitudine providebit? quasi dicat: Nequaquam, quum istud sit majus et laboriosius illo.
paras.en: [[3:5|But if a man know not how to rule his own house|Si quis autem domui suæ, id est domesticis, præesse nescit]], that is, his household, [[3:5|how shall he take care of the church of God?|quomodo Ecclesiæ Dei diligentiam habebit?]] that is, how will he provide for the whole congregation of the faithful with due solicitude? As if to say: by no means, since the one is greater and more laborious than the other.

paras.t: Non neophytum, id est noviter conversum, ne in superbiam elatus, id est tumore elationis inflatus ex subita promotione, se reputans aliis perfectiorem et Ecclesiæ pernecessarium, in judicium, id est reprobationem seu pœnam, incidat diaboli, qui ob suam elationem damnatus est.
paras.en: [[3:6|Not a neophyte|Non neophytum]], that is, one newly converted, [[3:6|lest, being puffed up with pride|ne in superbiam elatus]], that is, swollen with the tumour of elation from a sudden promotion, reckoning himself more perfect than others and most necessary to the Church, [[3:6|he fall into the judgment|in judicium]], that is, reprobation or punishment, [[3:6|of the devil|incidat diaboli]], who was condemned for his elation[[Is 14:12||]] [the margin gives Is. xiv, 12–15].

paras.t: Oportet autem illum et testimonium habere bonum ab his qui foris sunt, id est infidelibus et mundanis hominibus: hoc est, tanta virtutum excellentia necesse est eum fulgere, ut etiam a perversis laudetur, ita ut nemo valeat reprehendere eum, sicque facilius extranei a fide seu vita laudabili, ejus prædicationi consentiant; ut non in opprobrium incidat, id est contemptum, videlicet ne quis eum despiciat, et in laqueum diaboli, id est aliud quodcumque peccatum, quo dæmon capit atque illaqueat animam peccatricem.
paras.en: [[3:7|Moreover, he must have a good testimony of them who are without|Oportet autem illum et testimonium habere bonum ab his qui foris sunt]], that is, of unbelievers and worldly men: that is, he must shine with such excellence of virtues that he is praised even by the perverse, so that no one can reprehend him, and thus those who are strangers to the faith or to a praiseworthy life may the more readily consent to his preaching; [[3:7|lest he fall into reproach|ut non in opprobrium incidat]], that is, contempt, namely lest anyone despise him, [[3:7|and the snare of the devil|et in laqueum diaboli]], that is, any other sin whatever, by which the demon catches and ensnares the sinful soul.

paras.t: Insuper de statu et qualitate diaconorum subdit Apostolus: Diaconos similiter oportet esse pudicos, non bilingues, id est duabus loquelis utentes, videlicet aliter in præsentia, atque aliter in absentia loquentes: quales sunt adulatores, simulatores, et seminatores discordiæ. Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur: Susurro et bilinguis maledictus; multos enim turbavit pacem habentes. Talibus dicit Jacobus: Purificate corda, duplices animo.
paras.en: Further, the Apostle adds concerning the state and quality of deacons: [[3:8|Deacons in like manner|Diaconos similiter]] must be [[3:8|chaste|pudicos]], [[3:8|not double tongued|non bilingues]], that is, using two tongues, namely speaking one way in a man's presence and another in his absence: such are flatterers, dissemblers, and sowers of discord. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 28:15|The whisperer and the double tongue is accursed: for he hath troubled many that were at peace.|Susurro et bilinguis maledictus; multos enim turbavit pacem habentes]]. To such James says: [[Jas 4:8|purify your hearts, ye double minded|Purificate corda, duplices animo]].

paras.t: Non multo vino deditos, id est non vinolentos et ebriosos, ne sint mente obtusi, indiscreti ac lubrici, quoniam scriptum est: Luxuriosa res est vinum, et tumultuosa ebrietas; qui his delectatur, non erit sapiens. Non turpe lucrum, id est temporale commodum, sectantes, vel non vilius ementes, et carius vendentes. Turpe est enim huic professioni quæstibus studere. Habentes mysterium fidei, id est secreta fidei cognoscentes, in conscientia pura, videlicet, ne de sua scientia extollantur, vel secreta fidei curiose scrutentur.
paras.en: [[3:8|not given to much wine|Non multo vino deditos]], that is, not winebibbers and drunkards, lest they be dull of mind, indiscreet and given to lust, since it is written: [[Prov 20:1|Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness riotous: whosoever is delighted therewith, shall not be wise.|Luxuriosa res est vinum, et tumultuosa ebrietas; qui his delectatur, non erit sapiens]]. [[3:8|not greedy of filthy lucre|Non turpe lucrum]], that is, not pursuing temporal advantage, or not buying more cheaply and selling more dearly. For it is shameful for this profession to be intent on gain. [[3:9|Holding the mystery of faith|Habentes mysterium fidei]], that is, knowing the secrets of the faith, [[3:9|in a pure conscience|in conscientia pura]]: namely, so that they be not puffed up by their knowledge, nor pry curiously into the secrets of the faith.

paras.t: Et hi autem, id est diaconi et episcopi, probentur primum, id est, antequam promoveantur, examinentur si idonei sint; et sic probati et approbati, ministrent in suis officiis, nullum crimen, id est mortale peccatum, habentes.
paras.en: [[3:10|And let these also|Et hi autem]], that is, the deacons and the bishops, [[3:10|first be proved|probentur primum]], that is, before they are promoted let them be examined whether they are fit; [[3:10|and so|et sic]], proved and approved, [[3:10|let them minister|ministrent]] in their offices, [[3:10|having no crime|nullum crimen]], that is, no mortal sin.

paras.t: Mulieres similiter oportet esse pudicas, id est verecundas, honestas, foris compositas, non detrahentes, sobrias: ebrietas enim præcipue obest eis, quum sint debiles in rationis judicio; fideles in omnibus articulis fidei, vel in omnibus dictis et factis.
paras.en: [[3:11|The women in like manner|Mulieres similiter]] must be [[3:11|chaste|pudicas]], that is, modest, honourable, composed in their outward bearing[[1 Tim 2:9||]] [the margin gives I Tim. ii, 15; Denis's words are closer to 1 Tim 2:9], [[3:11|not slanderers|non detrahentes]], [[3:11|but sober|sobrias]]: for drunkenness is especially harmful to them, since they are weak in the judgment of reason; [[3:11|faithful in all things|fideles in omnibus]], that is, in all the articles of faith, or in all their words and deeds.
